name: Omar Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so public remarks can differ from private thoughts. Could you describe an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Omar, forty-three, and I lead the difficult wiring and repair jobs in homes and shops. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm often the one tracing a fault after the first explanation hasn't held up. I like a repair that lasts and an apprentice who can explain the checks, but I dislike a phone update that moves everything while I'm in somebody's kitchen.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Ruth books travel for a small agency, and our children are nine and twelve. We have a mortgage, twenty months of expenses saved, my higher-than-usual electrician's wage and plenty of other electrical employers nearby. We'd been looking at larger houses, but have signed nothing and paid no deposit. I never use AI; I keep a paper job diary and call the customer myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's finish the jobs people need and stop making the office system a test of everybody's character. A firm can use a small tool without asking the crew to change everything familiar. I'd keep teaching the apprentice beside the actual repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own work and our money feel secure in this picture. The wages cover the mortgage and family costs, and twenty months saved is a substantial cushion. I don't need the quiet version to make us rich; I like the ordinary work and the budget we already have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading repairs now and through the first year with the paper diary, direct customer calls and full checks. Ruth and I would keep the normal household budget and continue looking at written house costs without making a commitment. I'd ask for any compulsory new form to be shown by a person during paid time with normal weekly pay and hours protected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and glad to have something recognisable to get on with. I can enjoy a finished repair without needing the whole world to applaud a new way of doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check before agreeing a house purchase?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The actual mortgage offer, fees, moving costs and monthly bills, with Ruth agreeing the full budget. We'd leave the twenty-month emergency reserve intact and sign nothing until those conditions worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the reserve mean no need to earn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twenty months of costs isn't the rest of our lives. I'd rather use the reserve to make a careful decision than spend it proving we could afford a bigger front door.

I'd keep **practical apprentice teaching** alongside the real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say firms can compete with better tools, but somebody should tell staff what happens to their paid hours. Ruth's booking work is exactly the sort of thinking work on that card. I'd ask our office to explain a required change personally rather than pretend I understood it to make a meeting shorter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth's paid hours could shrink as booking and customer answers move to software. My physical repairs should be steadier. My wife's income is still household income, not spare change we can declare irrelevant. The reserve gives us room; it doesn't make me stop caring what my wife is being paid to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now Ruth and I would pause the larger-house search before any deposit and review actual wages and core bills monthly. I'd keep my repair work and ask the employer to explain required forms in paid time with normal weekly pay and hours protected, without using AI myself. In the first year we'd reopen the house question only with a written mortgage offer and full costs we both agreed were affordable, leaving the twenty-month reserve intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household wage, even though we have a strong cushion. I don't want to tell Ruth not to worry because my own toolbox still has somewhere to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does pausing the search actually change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We stop viewings and don't pay an agent or solicitor to start a purchase. It isn't a new deposit in the savings account; it is not taking on a bigger commitment while we check income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask Ruth to learn your trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not as a way to make the conversation easy for me. We'd check actual paid work and requirements, but Ruth would choose her own next step rather than be assigned a job from my tool bag.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking work changes in 2028 and physical robots follow around 2031, so both dates matter before we sign for a larger house. I'd ask employers for actual paid hours, not compliments about being experienced. I'd tell the children we're being careful, not asking them to fix the adults' future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of Ruth's booking income to go when thinking work becomes cheaper in 2028. My wage covers current essentials, but that would still be a large household-income loss, and later robots could reduce my own hours too. I'd be awake thinking about the second risk after the first wage had gone, even with twenty months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now we'd stop the larger-house plan and keep the current home and mortgage, with Ruth agreeing the decision. We'd write the budget using my actual wage and no assumed replacement income for Ruth. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep paid repairs, reviewing both wages and essential bills monthly before any new commitment, without turning the retained reserve into a new saving claim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing a large part of household income, not pretending the house is already lost. Our twenty-month reserve lets me ask questions; it doesn't stop me imagining two wages changing close together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the reserve to keep the larger-house plan alive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the current home works for us, even if the rooms are smaller than we'd like. I'd rather retain the cash than make the family depend on a wage I expect to disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help Ruth without inventing another job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Clear written hours and notice from the employer, and real paid-work offers with the requirements explained. I'd help compare actual terms if Ruth wanted, without putting an unoffered wage into the household budget.

fieldNote: His **alarm** follows expected household wage loss and possible later physical reductions, without claiming the present mortgage is already unaffordable.

steps.text: Stop larger-house plans with Ruth agreeing, keeping the current home and mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us check the household plan without asking a course advert to settle it. I'd favour paid apprenticeships and actual employer terms over telling people to be more adventurous. Thinking work arrives in 2031 and robots around 2034, so the longer warning still has both stages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect a large loss of Ruth's booking income in 2031, and no replacement wage is confirmed. My own pay covers current essentials, but a future robot reduction could make that harder at fifty-one around 2034. More time lets us avoid a bigger mortgage; the missing household wage still keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pause the house search now with Ruth agreeing and review our actual wages and essential costs quarterly. We'd make no purchase unless a real written mortgage offer, all costs and both our agreement left the twenty-month reserve intact and the monthly budget affordable. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep paid repairs and review the budget monthly, without a course enrolment or assumed new wage standing in for real earnings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed about the expected income loss, but with more time to choose what not to sign. I don't need the plan to sound ambitious; I need it to fit a bill that actually arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would refusing the bigger mortgage mean giving up every family plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we can keep the home that works and make smaller choices from actual income. I'd talk with the children about what matters to them rather than assume more rooms are the only way to care for a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you enrol in training because the deadline is farther away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not without a real practical task, provider, employer-paid fees and my full weekly wage protected during required teaching. I'm asking about terms, not saying I have accepted a place or become an AI user.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the children should learn to read real paid-learning offers instead of inherit a job because their father does it. I'd ask the same practical questions about wages, teaching and requirements for myself. A long warning is useful without turning every evening into homework for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our current work and household money look secure over the next few years with the major thinking change a decade away. I'll be fifty-three in 2036 and fifty-six when robots follow around 2039. The children will be nineteen and twenty-two in 2036, but I can't assume their wages, a cleared mortgage or a pension solve our later costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the house search paused now until Ruth and I agreed an affordable written mortgage offer and all costs, leaving the twenty-month reserve intact. We'd review actual household wages and essential costs quarterly, sooner if either changed. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep paid repairs and use actual monthly wages in the budget, without taking a possible job or training offer as an agreement until the terms were real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later work, but able to enjoy the present home without comparing it to a larger one. I can plan a family meal without asking the children to choose careers that make me feel safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would adult children's needs affect a future house decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only through what was actually needed and agreed then. I wouldn't copy today's school arrangements into a plan for adults, or assume an adult child could never need help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI now if it made the plan look more prepared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I never use it and I would ask a person to demonstrate any required process during paid time with normal weekly pay and hours protected. I'd rather admit how I learn than offer unpaid evenings to appear modern.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I expect most of Ruth's booking wage to go before any replacement is confirmed, with later robot risk to my repairs. Written paid hours and real practical work offers would help. If training were required, employer-paid fees and protected full weekly wages would matter more than a speech about being adaptable.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a family with savings is allowed to be worried without pretending it is already ruined. Our reserve is real, and so is the work Ruth does to earn a wage. Having a cushion doesn't mean my wife's lost wage would become imaginary.

headlineQuote: Having a cushion doesn't mean my wife's lost wage would become imaginary.
portrait: Omar is a **43-year-old crew leader** with a two-year technical diploma and master electrician's licence, handling difficult faults and final checks.
He has **twenty months saved**, higher pay, plentiful local firms, a mortgage and two schoolchildren with travel-booking wife Ruth.
He **never uses AI**, prefers a paper diary and wants required processes demonstrated personally during protected paid time.
Expected **booking-income loss** alarms him despite a strong reserve; his housing decisions preserve joint consent, actual mortgage terms and affordability.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings expected loss of most of Ruth's booking wage before confirmed replacement income, with later robot risk to repairs.
whatWouldHelp: **Written paid hours** and actual practical-work offers would help.
Required training should have **employer-paid fees** and protected full weekly wages, rather than an unchosen place or vague encouragement.
